title: Finally saw Killers Of The Flower Moon

commenti.body:
I felt that the pacing and duration was excellent. Scorsese clearly wants to show us the events, as plainly and that, while the audience tries to figure out and let themselves wonder in horror by the cold actions of souless capitalists, and the story of a man being slowly corrupted—did he ever had a heart or did he loose himself in the process? When does love become abuse?

Scorsese won't let the viewer skip the tragedy (for all the people who finished their popcorn within the first 30 minutes of the film). But about that ending... (and we will get into spoilers, this is r/truefilm)

He can't help but feel that the cinematic image still isn't enough to tell some kind of stories—perhaps any story. He's aware of the film's own inadequacy, aware of the industry he's in, afraid of failing at such a massive subject, of the celluloid's own futiliness under a modern audience filled with futil content. He puts himself in such a madness he can't help but break his own film, and with the necessesity of warning every viewer, he lets the final image of his film be a document of the Osage tribe living to this day.

That is a super interesting point- and it makes sense. I was not only surprised by the twist of the theatre, but also when he himself breaks into the movie… I did ask why he felt the need to and your perspective helps shed light on that. 
I also wonder if it brought it into the real world (or real time) for us viewers with the repeated phrase… “no investigation …” it just felt like geesh these atrocities are a literal stain on our country that began with Native peoples and continue to this day. These injustices… 
Thanks for your feedback! I love hearing everyone’s thoughts in this community. It’s really makes the experience more enjoyable for me :)

The acting is really superb on everyone’s part, but Lily Gladstone is a revelation. I usually don’t like DiCaprio but he acted his ass off and the part suited him well, it’s just that Gladstone overshadowed him and DeNiro, blew ‘em off the screen. The Oscar’s definitely hers to lose.

I thought KOTFM was more interesting than Oppenheimer, perhaps partially because I hadn't read the book so it was all new to me. I knew enough about Oppenheimer to know what to expect.

But I also don't like how impersonal Nolan films can feel. I don't think his more plot driven rather than character driven style is necessarily well suited for a biopic. It would have benefited from more intimacy, which is something Scorsese is great at.  

I kinda wonder if they should have traded places. KOTFM could have benefited from feeling "bigger", which is something Nolan excels at.. It would be interesting to see what a Scorsese Oppenheimer and a Nolan KOTFM would look like.

Yea I’m with you there. Her face is captivating and she holds you with her eyes in a really unique way! I was super impressed with her. I feel like she said so much with her eyes and body language… swoon! 
I know DiCaprio can often be accused of overacting or whatever but I dunno. I’ve seen most of his movies, I think he’s great. He was solid in this pic and to me DeNiro’s face is so terrifying in this movie.

That’s also a great point. There was like a general get to know the characters… like a broad overview, but no in a deeply personal way. Which I gather from previous commentary on here that it is the Nolan way… I never really noticed it before so it kinda tracks to me what you’re saying about the genre of film. Maybe the biopic route kinda needs more of a deep dive, lol. Seems obvious but still. 

I do push back though on the whole idea of a film needing to be big in order to be good or in order to be Oscar worthy. If it serves the story, of course… but to me I didn’t feel KOTFM suffered from a lack of bigness at all. It didn’t even register in my mind at all. The story was so good from the get I was just sucked in. 
In fact so many of the other noms (like anatomy or past lives, even the holdovers) are the opposite of big to me and instead invite you into this space. It’s intimate, vulnerable, honest. Both styles are great but man, when it’s executed well, I will pick the more intimate or “smaller” feel movie every time. Just me though, probably not the Academy, lol. But I wish that there was more openness to that…
Despite the length of KOTFM, my girlfriend and her friend both made it through without going to the restroom, which is rare for them even in shorter films. It had us all enthralled.

I’ve seen all the best picture nominees except for Maestro. In order of best to worst, I’d rank them:

Poor Things  
Past Lives  
The Holdovers  
The Zone of Interest  
Oppenheimer  
Barbie
Anatomy of a Fall
American Fiction
Killers of the Flower Moon

To be clear, I liked all of these, and Poor Things and Past Lives made my top four of 2023 (and both will end up on my all time favorites list). I disagree with Oppenheimer's runtime not being well-handled, as someone with a low attention span who was still engrossed throughout the entirety of the film.

Yet, I very much agree on Killers of the Flower Moon's runtime being well-executed and much more so than what most claim it to be. It is not meant to be a murder mystery of sorts, which it seems was the set of expectations the film's detractors had of the film. Yet what the film is a slow-burn drama over seeing how this man was corrupted by his own greed and foolishness into doing the horrible things he did, and most importantly the woman who suffered and lost her family to the people she trusted. The tragedy of it is emphasised and presented with powerful honesty and a clear respect to the Osage people, with every scene absolutely essential to contributing to this. Most notably, the ending was just beautiful and the closest I've gotten this year to tearing up, and I'm not even part of the community. Either KOTFM or Oppie had my favourite ending of the year, and I'm glad the former's song is nominated and would be most thrilled if it won.

My only two problems of the film is that the score, as good as it was, did become mildly repetitive in the second half and that Brendan Fraiser's inclusion was quite forced in. Other than these two criticisms, the film was great and one of the best of the year. It should've been nominated for Best Adapted Screenplay, quite honestly and DiCaprio should've gotten nominated over two of the five selections.

As for the other BP nominees, I have seen them all. My ranking would roughly resemble as such:

1. Poor Things (10/10)
2. Zone of Interest (9/10)
3. Oppenheimer (9/10)
4. Past Lives (9/10)
5. Anatomy of a Fall (8-9/10)
6. Killers of the Flower Moon (8/10)
7. Barbie (7-8/10)
8. The Holdovers (7/10)
9. American Fiction (6/10)
10. Maestro (6/10)

Zone of Interest is a unique and brilliant take on Holocaust films, and is rather comfortably the best of director Johnathon Glazer's filmography.

It's a truly excellent film on every front. It's a superficially strange and "insane", yet ambitious and intricately-crafted film that is visually and musically eclectic. 

The performances are immensely energetic, distinct and nuanced, all brilliantly depicting complex characters. Stone and Ruffalo in particular deliver career-best performances. It's a thematically-rich and challenging film about discovery, certainly quite... explicit, yet it's humanised by its charmingly quirky humour with Lanthimos' trademark edge. It's quite possibly the most visually stunning film of the year, with grand sets, dynamic costuming and rich, versatile use of colour that is helmed under jaw-dropping cinematography. 

Some people complain about it being "misogynistic" and "too long", but I didn't experience those issues, since the length is justified by just how out-there an experience the film offers, yet it maintains its coherence and depth. I'm not getting into the conversation over the former criticism, since its just insecure Twitterers projecting their unrelated politics onto film like what happened with Barbie. 

I honestly can't think of a single fault of this film, any time its intent is blundered in execution or any choice that didn't sit right with me. If you enjoy Lanthimos' previous films, then I highly recommend it as the best of his work yet.

I might be overhyping it, as I'm aware some people can have their opinion significantly skewed to be more critical when they believe a hyped-up film is going to change their lives. So I do recommend that you keep your expectations in check, but I believe you will at least be able to find something respect about the film.

It's a more deserving nomination for BP than Maestro, I can state that very confidently.

He garnered criticism for still limiting the depiction of the Osage and their experience, but he would have been criticized had he done that as well. Instead, he made a movie where he focuses on acknowledging the harm done to the Osage loud and clear, and it is large and magnificent in the process.

The Osage died, they weren't even mentioned, nobody got really punished. The only existence of these real, lived tragedies, are in the form of radio stories and movies, entertainment. It really hammers home the injustice and inequity that has been done to the many indigenous communities in the continent.

I’m now only missing American fiction (coming to my local theatre this week) and maestro and I have to say I’ve generally been blown away by the quality (and originality) of the best pic noms this year. 
I’m someone that was charmed by Oppenheimer, but i think killers is a better movie, but just by a hair. Scorsese’s cameo was such an expertly done choice that made me very emotional on both watches, but as far as favourites I think Zone of Interest and Anatomy of a Fall have been the most underrated (not a coincidence that both have Huller at the helm). Though vastly different in content both stuck with me very strongly. Zone was such a jarring mix of stillness and sound and told a well known story in a new way, choosing to show us the normalcy of monsters instead of othering them from ourselves, which I find exceptionally important in the world today. 

Anatomy of a fall worked so well because we aren’t hand fed every detail, and frankly was a much better feminist film than Barbie (as was poor things imo). 

I also particularly loved Past Lives but that’s one that I felt the beating heart of the story was just something that spoke to me, and was a very strong movie, but I guess less ‘flashy’ than the rest
